strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes concept drift in VAD, distinguishing it from open-set and domain generalization settings. The mathematical formulation P(Y|V,Z)→Y elegantly captures changing anomaly definitions.

Significant dataset contribution: PreVAD (35,279 videos) is the largest VAD dataset to date with multi-level taxonomy, anomaly descriptions, and diverse sources. The scalable curation pipeline leveraging MLLMs demonstrates a practical approach to large-scale data collection.

Strong and consistent empirical results: Achieves SOTA across all seven test datasets with 20-32% improvements on XD-Violence. Demonstrates superior robustness to concept drift (Protocol 2) compared to multi-modal and LLM-based baselines.

Comprehensive evaluation with dual protocols: Protocol 1 evaluates cross-domain generalization; Protocol 2 specifically assesses concept drift robustness. Two evaluation settings provide complementary evidence of the method's effectiveness.

Reasonable technical approach addressing real challenges: Dynamic video synthesis mitigates web-sourced data bias; contrastive learning with hard negative mining enhances feature discrimination. Design choices are pragmatic.

Clear presentation with strong motivation: Paper is well-written with effective visualizations (e.g., Fig. 1's paradigm comparison, Fig. 4's concept drift visualization). Comprehensive supplementary materials support reproducibility.
Computational efficiency: Method is significantly faster than LLM-based baselines (minutes vs. hours), making it practical for real applications.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: Authors acknowledge adopting a 'simplified network' design. Core components (vanilla Transformer encoder, co-attention fusion, linear detection head) are standard. Technical contribution at architecture level is incremental relative to VadCLIP.

Dataset quality concerns: Heavy reliance on automatic MLLM annotation for descriptions and cleansing. LLM hallucinations mentioned but not quantitatively evaluated. No inter-annotator agreement metrics reported. ~25% of retrieved videos filtered without detailed analysis of criteria.

Evaluation gaps on concept drift: Protocol 2 uses only 5 random subsets per dataset; no systematic analysis of which definition changes are most challenging. Only XD-Violence and MSAD evaluated under Protocol 2, limiting generalizability of concept drift findings.

Prompt engineering requirement: All experiments use manual prompts based on known dataset categories. No evaluation on truly user-provided definitions with different phrasings. Table E shows video-specific descriptions outperform (83.03 vs 81.12), but these are unavailable in deployment.

Absence of statistical significance testing: Results presented as single numbers without error bars, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests. Unclear if improvements are statistically significant or result of single runs.

Dynamic video synthesis design lacks justification: Random segment selection (Algorithm 1) unclear how temporal coherence is preserved. Heuristic k-NN based synthesis lacks theoretical grounding. No analysis of whether improvements come from synthesis validity vs. simple data augmentation.

Shallow analysis of failure modes: Only one example of concept drift handling (Fig. 4). No systematic analysis of which definition changes or anomaly types challenge the method. Unclear distinction between natural distribution shifts vs. true concept drift.

Reproducibility constraints: Dataset and code promised but unavailable at review time. Reproducibility claims depend on future release. Dataset quality issues (MLLM-based annotation) cannot be fully verified independently.
